items.title: The Big Picture
items.subtitle: Cars: How They Work and How to Fix Them ·
items.body: A car is a team of systems with one job: turn stored energy into motion you can steer and stop. This lesson gives you the map. Every later lesson zooms in on one part of it.

systems.name: Engine
systems.desc: Burns fuel and air to turn the crankshaft.

systems.name: Air, fuel and spark
systems.desc: Air filter, fuel tank, lines, injectors and ignition.

systems.name: Cooling and lubrication
systems.desc: Radiator, hoses, fan and coolant; oil keeps parts apart.

systems.name: Exhaust and emissions
systems.desc: Pipes, catalytic converter and muffler carry and clean the exhaust.

systems.name: Transmission and drivetrain
systems.desc: Transmission, driveshaft and differential carry power to the wheels.

systems.name: Electric drive
systems.desc: Traction battery, power electronics, motor, charge port and thermal system.

systems.name: Compressed-air tanks
systems.desc: Carbon-fiber-wrapped tanks (COPVs) tucked into every spare space; about 600 liters of compressed air, says Tesla’s Lars Moravy.

systems.name: Valves and gas lines
systems.desc: Lines carry the gas to each thruster, and fast valves open and close it.

systems.name: Rear thrusters (Thrust)
systems.desc: Cold-gas nozzles at the back. They throw air backward, so the car is pushed forward.

systems.name: Thrusters all around (Rocket)
systems.desc: On the Rocket version, nozzles around the body push up and spin the car. Not approved for public roads, per Tesla’s page.

systems.name: Suction fans and skirts
systems.desc: Fans pull air from under the car and skirts seal it off, so the air above presses the car down.

systems.name: Electrical system
systems.desc: Battery, alternator or DC/DC converter, wiring, lights and fuses.

systems.name: Brakes
systems.desc: Master cylinder, lines, calipers and rotors at each wheel.

systems.name: Steering and suspension
systems.desc: Springs, shocks, steering column and rack.

systems.name: Wheels and tires
systems.desc: The only parts that touch the road.

items.title: The Engine
items.subtitle: Cars: How They Work and How to Fix Them ·
items.body: An engine is an air pump that powers itself. It pulls in air and fuel, squeezes them, burns them, and pushes out what’s left, over and over, many times every second. Watch it happen, then meet each part.

items.title: Air, Fuel and Spark
items.subtitle: Cars: How They Work and How to Fix Them ·
items.body: A gasoline engine needs three things at once: the right amount of air, the right amount of fuel for that air, and a spark at the right instant. A computer juggles all three, adjusting them constantly as you drive.

items.title: The Electrical System

items.body: Every modern car runs on electricity, even one that burns gasoline. The battery starts the engine, the alternator keeps everything powered once it’s running, and a web of wires, fuses and grounds carries current to every light, sensor and computer.

items.title: Brakes
items.subtitle: Cars: How They Work and How to Fix Them ·
items.body: Brakes turn the energy of a moving car into heat. Your foot supplies only a small push; a lever and a hydraulic system multiply it into thousands of pounds of squeeze at the wheels.

items.title: Steering, Suspension and Alignment
items.subtitle: Cars: How They Work and How to Fix Them ·
items.body: The suspension keeps the tires pressed to the road while the body rides smoothly over bumps, and the steering points the front wheels where you want to go. Alignment is the set of small angles that makes it all track straight.

items.title: Hybrids and Electric Cars
items.subtitle: Cars: How They Work and How to Fix Them ·
items.body: Electric drive replaces or helps the engine with motors that run on a high-voltage battery. Fewer moving parts and no oil changes make an electric car simpler to maintain, but its high-voltage system is one area where only trained technicians belong.

systems.name: Engine
systems.desc: Burns fuel and air to turn the crankshaft.

systems.name: Air, fuel and spark
systems.desc: Air filter, fuel tank, lines, injectors and ignition.

systems.name: Cooling and lubrication
systems.desc: Radiator, hoses, fan and coolant; oil keeps parts apart.

systems.name: Exhaust and emissions
systems.desc: Pipes, catalytic converter and muffler carry and clean the exhaust.

systems.name: Transmission and drivetrain
systems.desc: Transmission, driveshaft and differential carry power to the wheels.

systems.name: Electric drive
systems.desc: Traction battery, power electronics, motor, charge port and thermal system.

systems.name: Compressed-air tanks
systems.desc: Carbon-fiber-wrapped tanks (COPVs) tucked into every spare space; about 600 liters of compressed air, says Tesla’s Lars Moravy.

systems.name: Valves and gas lines
systems.desc: Lines carry the gas to each thruster, and fast valves open and close it.

systems.name: Rear thrusters (Thrust)
systems.desc: Cold-gas nozzles at the back. They throw air backward, so the car is pushed forward.

systems.name: Thrusters all around (Rocket)
systems.desc: On the Rocket version, nozzles around the body push up and spin the car. Not approved for public roads, per Tesla’s page.

systems.name: Suction fans and skirts
systems.desc: Fans pull air from under the car and skirts seal it off, so the air above presses the car down.

systems.name: Electrical system
systems.desc: Battery, alternator or DC/DC converter, wiring, lights and fuses.

systems.name: Brakes
systems.desc: Master cylinder, lines, calipers and rotors at each wheel.

systems.name: Steering and suspension
systems.desc: Springs, shocks, steering column and rack.

systems.name: Wheels and tires
systems.desc: The only parts that touch the road.

items.title: Thrusters and Fans on the 2026 Roadster
items.subtitle: Cars: How They Work and How to Fix Them ·
items.body: Tesla’s new Roadster adds two things no road car has had: thrusters that push it with jets of compressed air, and fans that suck it onto the road. Here’s what was announced, what Tesla’s patent covers, and the physics of how both work, with simulators you can run yourself.

items.title: Doing Your Own Work
items.subtitle: Cars: How They Work and How to Fix Them ·
items.body: Doing your own car work saves money and teaches you how your car is put together. Start with simple checks, build skill one rung at a time, and know which jobs belong to trained professionals.

systems.name: Engine
systems.desc: Burns fuel and air to turn the crankshaft.

systems.name: Air, fuel and spark
systems.desc: Air filter, fuel tank, lines, injectors and ignition.

systems.name: Cooling and lubrication
systems.desc: Radiator, hoses, fan and coolant; oil keeps parts apart.

systems.name: Exhaust and emissions
systems.desc: Pipes, catalytic converter and muffler carry and clean the exhaust.

systems.name: Transmission and drivetrain
systems.desc: Transmission, driveshaft and differential carry power to the wheels.

systems.name: Electric drive
systems.desc: Traction battery, power electronics, motor, charge port and thermal system.

systems.name: Compressed-air tanks
systems.desc: Carbon-fiber-wrapped tanks (COPVs) tucked into every spare space; about 600 liters of compressed air, says Tesla’s Lars Moravy.

systems.name: Valves and gas lines
systems.desc: Lines carry the gas to each thruster, and fast valves open and close it.

systems.name: Rear thrusters (Thrust)
systems.desc: Cold-gas nozzles at the back. They throw air backward, so the car is pushed forward.

systems.name: Thrusters all around (Rocket)
systems.desc: On the Rocket version, nozzles around the body push up and spin the car. Not approved for public roads, per Tesla’s page.

systems.name: Suction fans and skirts
systems.desc: Fans pull air from under the car and skirts seal it off, so the air above presses the car down.

systems.name: Electrical system
systems.desc: Battery, alternator or DC/DC converter, wiring, lights and fuses.

systems.name: Brakes
systems.desc: Master cylinder, lines, calipers and rotors at each wheel.

systems.name: Steering and suspension
systems.desc: Springs, shocks, steering column and rack.

systems.name: Wheels and tires
systems.desc: The only parts that touch the road.

items.title: The Big Picture
items.subtitle: Construction: How a House Is Built ·
items.body: A house is built from the ground up, in an order that lets each crew work on what the last one finished. This lesson walks through that order, meets the people who do each part, and explains the rules that keep the result safe. The map shows every system in one house.

systems.name: Site and drainage
systems.desc: Grading and downspouts that carry water away from the house.

systems.name: Foundation
systems.desc: Footings, walls, slab and drain tile: the house’s weight goes into the soil here.

systems.name: Floor and wall framing
systems.desc: Sill plate, joists, studs, plates and headers: the skeleton that carries the loads.

systems.name: Roof
systems.desc: Trusses carry the roof; sheathing, shingles and flashing shed the water.

systems.name: Rough-ins
systems.desc: Pipes, wires and ducts run through the open framing (see the Plumbing, Electrical and HVAC courses).

systems.name: Envelope
systems.desc: Siding, house wrap and insulation control water, air, vapor and heat.

systems.name: Windows and doors
systems.desc: Flashed into the walls so they let in light and people, not weather.

systems.name: Interior finishes
systems.desc: Drywall, trim, floors, paint and stairs.

items.title: Loads and Structure
items.subtitle: Construction: How a House Is Built ·
items.body: Every pound in a house, from the shingles to the people in the kitchen, has to find its way down to the ground. Builders call that route the load path. This lesson follows it, names the four ways a part can be loaded, and shows why a deeper joist is so much stiffer.

items.subtitle: Construction: How a House Is Built ·
items.body: A foundation has two jobs. It spreads the weight of the house over enough soil to hold it, and it keeps the wood frame up out of the wet ground. Both start with the site: the soil and, above all, where the water goes.

items.title: The Building Envelope
items.subtitle: Construction: How a House Is Built ·
items.body: The envelope is everything that separates inside from outside: the foundation, walls, windows, doors and roof. A good one controls four things: liquid water, air, water vapor and heat. This lesson takes them one at a time.

systems.name: Site and drainage

systems.name: Floor and wall framing

systems.name: Roof
systems.desc: Trusses carry the roof; sheathing, shingles and flashing shed the water.

systems.desc: Pipes, wires and ducts run through the open framing (see the Plumbing, Electrical and HVAC courses).

systems.name: Envelope
systems.desc: Siding, house wrap and insulation control water, air, vapor and heat.

systems.name: Windows and doors
systems.desc: Flashed into the walls so they let in light and people, not weather.

items.subtitle: Construction: How a House Is Built ·
items.body: A lot of what goes wrong with houses comes back to water. This lesson explains where it comes from, the four ways it moves, why cold surfaces sweat, and how good details keep wood dry and mold away.

items.title: The Big Picture: From Power Plant to Outlet
items.subtitle: Electrical: How Power Gets to Your Outlets ·
items.body: Flip a switch and the light comes on at once. Behind that switch is a chain of machines and wires that starts at a power plant, often far away. This lesson follows electricity from the plant to your outlet and gives you a map of the electrical system in a house. Every later lesson zooms in on one part of it.

systems.desc: 120-volt circuits wired in parallel from the panel to each room.

items.title: Volts, Amps, Ohms and Watts
items.subtitle: Electrical: How Power Gets to Your Outlets ·
items.body: Four little words do most of the work in electricity: volts, amps, ohms and watts. Once you know how they fit together, you can read an appliance label, predict when a breaker will trip, and check your electric bill. This lesson gives you the formulas and the reasons behind them.

items.title: The Service and the Panel
items.subtitle: Electrical: How Power Gets to Your Outlets ·
items.body: The main panel is the heart of a home’s electrical system. Power from the utility comes in through the meter, passes through the main breaker, and is split up into branch circuits, each guarded by its own breaker. This lesson explains every part and how a breaker knows when to trip. It isn’t a how-to: work inside a panel belongs with a licensed electrician.

items.title: Grounding and Bonding
items.subtitle: Electrical: How Power Gets to Your Outlets ·
items.body: Most of the time the ground wire does nothing at all. It’s there for the day something goes wrong, such as a frayed hot wire touching the metal case of a tool. This lesson explains how grounding and bonding turn that dangerous moment into a tripped breaker, and why your plugs are shaped the way they are.

items.title: GFCIs, AFCIs and Other Protection
items.subtitle: Electrical: How Power Gets to Your Outlets ·
items.body: A breaker protects the wires, but it can’t protect a person: the current that can kill you is far too small for a breaker to notice. Two smarter devices fill the gap. The GFCI guards against shock and the AFCI guards against fires from arcing. This lesson shows how each one works, along with the other safety devices in a modern home.

items.title: Doing Your Own Work
items.subtitle: Electrical: How Power Gets to Your Outlets ·
items.body: Electrical work is the one home trade where a small mistake can hide inside a wall for years and then start a fire, or hurt someone right away. That’s why it’s the most regulated. This lesson explains who is allowed to do what, the tools worth owning, and a ladder of skills from your first safe jobs to the ones that belong with a licensed electrician.

items.title: The Big Picture
items.subtitle: HVAC: Heating, Cooling and Fresh Air ·
items.body: Heat always flows from warmer things to colder things, all by itself. In winter it leaks out of your house; in summer it leaks in. A heating and cooling system pushes back: it adds heat or carries it away, swaps stale air for fresh, and keeps the air from getting too damp. This lesson gives you the map, and every later lesson zooms in on one part of it.

systems.name: Air conditioner

systems.name: Heat pump
systems.desc: One outdoor unit heats and cools; the indoor air handler holds the coil, the blower and backup heat.

systems.name: Refrigerant lines
systems.desc: Two copper lines carry refrigerant between the outdoor unit and the indoor coil.

systems.name: Ducts and filter
systems.desc: Supply ducts and registers deliver air; a return grille and duct bring it back through the filter.

systems.name: Ventilation and CO alarms
systems.desc: Bath fan, kitchen hood, a heat recovery ventilator and a CO alarm outside the bedroom.

systems.name: Thermostat and controls
systems.desc: The thermostat and the low-voltage wires that tell the equipment when to run.

systems.name: Insulation and air sealing
systems.desc: Attic and wall insulation and sealed gaps: the house itself, which sets how much heating and cooling it needs.

items.title: The Refrigeration Cycle
items.subtitle: HVAC: Heating, Cooling and Fresh Air ·
items.body: Air conditioners, heat pumps, refrigerators and dehumidifiers all run the same loop. A fluid boils where it’s cold, soaking up heat; a compressor squeezes it; then it condenses where it’s warm and gives the heat away. This is the heart of the course.

items.title: Heat Pumps
items.subtitle: HVAC: Heating, Cooling and Fresh Air ·
items.body: A heat pump is an air conditioner that can run backward. In winter it pulls heat out of cold outdoor air, or out of the ground, and pumps it inside. Because it moves heat instead of making it, it can deliver several times more heat than the electricity it uses.

items.body: The furnace or heat pump makes the heating and cooling; the blower and ducts deliver it. A great furnace on bad ducts still leaves rooms too hot, too cold or dusty, and wastes a good share of the energy you pay for.

items.title: Ventilation and Indoor Air
items.subtitle: HVAC: Heating, Cooling and Fresh Air ·

items.subtitle: HVAC: Heating, Cooling and Fresh Air ·

items.title: The Big Picture
items.subtitle: Plumbing: How Water Gets In and Out of a House ·
items.body: A house has two plumbing systems that must never mix. One brings clean water in under pressure. The other carries used water and waste away by gravity, with vents that let air in. This lesson gives you the map; every later lesson zooms in on one part of it.

systems.name: Water service, meter and main shutoff
systems.desc: The service line from the street main, the curb stop, the meter, your main shutoff valve and the pressure-reducing valve.

systems.name: Cold water lines
systems.desc: Pipes full of water under pressure, branching to every fixture and to the water heater.

systems.name: Water heater and hot lines
systems.desc: The water heater and the hot lines that run beside the cold ones.

systems.name: Gas line
systems.desc: Gas from the meter to the water heater and furnace. Gas work is for licensed pros.

systems.name: Fixtures and appliances
systems.desc: Sinks, the toilet, the tub and the clothes washer: where water is used.

systems.name: Drains, traps and the building drain
systems.desc: Traps under each fixture, branch drains, the stack and the building drain, all sloped downhill.

systems.name: Vents
systems.desc: Pipes open above the roof that let air into the drains so traps keep their water.

systems.name: Building sewer
systems.desc: Carries everything from the house to the public sewer main (or a septic tank).

items.title: Drains, Traps and Vents
items.subtitle: Plumbing: How Water Gets In and Out of a House ·
items.body: Drains look simple: water goes down. But a drain system has a hidden job. It has to carry waste away while blocking sewer gas from coming back up, and it does that with nothing more than a bend of pipe, a little water, and a pipe through the roof.

items.title: Fixtures and How They Work
items.subtitle: Plumbing: How Water Gets In and Out of a House ·
items.body: Fixtures are where you meet the plumbing. A toilet is a little machine built from a float, a valve and a siphon. A faucet is a valve you can grab. A shower valve quietly protects you from scalding. Once you know how they work, most of their problems make sense.

items.subtitle: Plumbing: How Water Gets In and Out of a House ·
items.body: Water heating is the second-largest energy expense in the average American home, according to the Department of Energy. A tank heater is simple inside, but it holds a lot of hot water under pressure, so it has one safety part everyone should understand: the temperature-and-pressure relief valve.

items.title: Leaks and Water Use
items.subtitle: Plumbing: How Water Gets In and Out of a House ·
items.body: A drip doesn’t look like much. But EPA says the average household’s leaks can waste more than 9,300 gallons a year, and nationwide household leaks waste nearly a trillion gallons. Finding them takes two free tests and a little detective work.

items.title: Clogs, Frozen Pipes and Noisy Pipes
items.subtitle: Plumbing: How Water Gets In and Out of a House ·
items.body: Most plumbing calls come down to a handful of everyday problems: a drain that won’t drain, a pipe that froze, pressure that dropped, or pipes that bang. Each has a simple bit of physics behind it.

items.title: Gas Piping and Gas Appliances
items.subtitle: Plumbing: How Water Gets In and Out of a House ·
items.body: Many plumbers also run the gas lines that feed water heaters, furnaces, ranges and dryers. Gas work is a different world from water: a leak isn’t a puddle, it’s a fire or explosion risk, and a bad vent can fill a house with carbon monoxide. This lesson explains how the system works and why it belongs to licensed pros. It is not a how-to.

items.title: Doing Your Own Work
items.subtitle: Plumbing: How Water Gets In and Out of a House ·
items.body: A lot of plumbing is within reach: clearing a clog, fixing a running toilet, cleaning an aerator, finding a leak. Some of it isn’t, by law or by risk. This lesson helps you tell the difference and build skill one rung at a time.

systems.name: Water service, meter and main shutoff
systems.desc: The service line from the street main, the curb stop, the meter, your main shutoff valve and the pressure-reducing valve.

systems.name: Cold water lines
systems.desc: Pipes full of water under pressure, branching to every fixture and to the water heater.

systems.name: Water heater and hot lines
systems.desc: The water heater and the hot lines that run beside the cold ones.

systems.name: Gas line
systems.desc: Gas from the meter to the water heater and furnace. Gas work is for licensed pros.

systems.name: Fixtures and appliances
systems.desc: Sinks, the toilet, the tub and the clothes washer: where water is used.

systems.name: Drains, traps and the building drain
systems.desc: Traps under each fixture, branch drains, the stack and the building drain, all sloped downhill.

systems.name: Vents
systems.desc: Pipes open above the roof that let air into the drains so traps keep their water.

systems.name: Building sewer
systems.desc: Carries everything from the house to the public sewer main (or a septic tank).

items.title: Careers in Plumbing
items.subtitle: Plumbing: How Water Gets In and Out of a House ·
items.body: Every building needs water in and waste out, and somebody has to design, install and fix it. Plumbing is one of the skilled trades you can learn while you earn, through a paid apprenticeship, and it can lead to a license, a business of your own, or both.
